items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the environmental conservation law and the state finance law, in relation to the regional land banks for projects on state land in the forest preserve
items.lawCode: Add §9-0309, En Con L; amd §97-e, St Fin L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S8027

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the environmental conservation law
and the state finance law, in relation to the regional land banks for
projects on state land in the forest preserve

 PURPOSE :

The purpose of this bill is to amend the Environmental Conservation
Law (ECL) to allow the use of state lands for public utilities and
bike paths and to establish regional land banks for local roads,
bridges, public water supplies and public utilities in the Adirondacks
and Catskills pursuant to an amendment to Article XIV of the
Constitution, and the State Finance Law in relation to the Forest
Preserve Expansion Fund.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of this bill adds a new ECL § 9-0309, "Use of certain state
lands in forest preserve counties for public utilities and regional
land bank for projects on state lands." This section would allow
utility lines to be buried or co-located within the maintained width
of highways that traverse state lands and allow construction of bike
paths in such areas.

This section would also establish two land banks in forest preserve
counties, 500 acres for the Adirondack region and 250 acres for the
Catskill region. The land banks could be available to towns, counties,
public water supplies and public utilities for highway, bridge, bike
path, environmental infrastructure, water supply, and public utility
projects where no feasible alternative exists. An individual project
would be limited to no more than five acres. No more than ten acres in
total could be used by an individual town or fifteen acres by an
individual county, unless authorized by the legislature. Any project
sponsor that uses land from the land bank would be required to pay an
amount equal to the value of the state lands or easement into an
account for acquisitions to the forest preserve and funds collected
would be used to purchase land for addition to the forest preserve.
Any public utility or water supply project would have to be approved
by the town or towns where the project is proposed.

DEC would have to acquire 750 acres of land for addition to the forest
preserve which would be classified as wilderness prior to allowing the
use of the land bank.

Section 2 of this bill amends State Finance Law § 97-e to allow for
moneys received for a regional land bank transaction to be deposited
into the forest preserve expansion fund. This section also clarifies
that the moneys in the fund shall be used for the acquisition of
additional lands for the forest preserve as well as the conservation
of forest and wild life in forest preserve counties.

Section 3 of this bill provides that the act is effective upon passage
of a constitutional amendment authorizing the establishment of a
forest preserve land bank for public project.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Article XIV of the State Constitution prevents state lands, including
forest preserve, reforestation areas, and wildlife management areas,
in Adirondack and Catskill counties from being leased, sold or
exchanged and prohibits them from being taken by any public or private
corporation. Thus, alienation of these lands requires a Constitutional
Amendment, passed by two successive, separately elected legislatures
and ratified by the electorate at a general election. This process is
intended to set a high standard for the alienation of state lands.
However, this process is overly cumbersome, time consuming and
expensive for small communities that need small amounts of state land
for water supply, road and utility projects critical to the public
health and safety.

The state's land acquisition program has caused the forest preserve to
nearly quadruple in size since 1895, when the forest preserve was
first given constitutional protection. In 1895, the preserve included
750,000 acres; now, the preserve includes nearly 3,000,000 acres. In
one Adirondack town, Arietta, the State owns 93 percent of the land,
while in Hamilton County the State owns more than 50 percent of the
land. The presence of state land has frustrated the siting of basic
public projects. Sometimes, due to land ownership patterns, the only
feasible alternative is to site a project on state land. The inability
to use State land can also result in the loss of funding for essential
projects.

For example, in 2008 the town of Elizabethtown received $6.4 million
in federal funding to install and upgrade much needed sewer lines.
However, the town discovered late in the process that the lines would
cross a small area of forest preserve land. The town did not have the
resources necessary to advance an amendment allowing the lines to
cross the preserve lands. Moreover, there was a three year limit on
federal grant funds for the project and, because first and second
passage of the joint resolution by the legislature requires passage in
two separate sessions of the legislature and then a vote of the
people, an individual, site-specific Constitutional Amendment could
not be secured before funding for the project expired. Therefore,
federal funding for the project was lost and the needed sewer line
project has yet to be completed.

A second example of where the anti-alienation provisions in Article
XIV have prevented an important public health and safety project from
moving forward is the relocation of the Middleton Bridge in the Town
of Horicon. The existing bridge crossing the Schroon River was closed
due to structural problems and a new replacement bridge is needed.
However, the new bridge needs to be located upstream from the existing
bridge because the road leading to the existing bridge is subject to
periodic flooding of the river. The best location for the new bridge
would cross the river where the state owns both river banks, and the
state land is subject to Article XIV's anti-alienation provisions. As
a result, the bridge cannot be constructed without a constitutional
amendment. The Town of Horicon lacks the resources to secure first and
second legislative passage of an amendment and to produce the
educational materials necessary to inform the voters of the State as
to the need for the bridge. Consequently, a replacement bridge has not
been built. Access to the residences on the east side of the river is
currently by a lengthy, indirect route, creating an unreasonable
emergency responder response time.

Since 1894, a small handful of amendments to Article XIV have been
passed to address public health, safety and welfare issues. These
amendments have normally been site specific and required land
exchanges whereby the State receives, for inclusion in the forest
preserve, land that is greater in value and acreage than the land that
is being taken out of the forest preserve:

In 2007, the voters approved an amendment allowing the Town of Long
Lake to acquire one acre of forest preserve land for the siting of
drinking water wells to provide potable water to the hamlet of
Raquette Lake in exchange for not less than 12 acres of land at least
equal in value to the acre conveyed to the Town. Raquette Lake had
been using unfiltered water from the local reservoir, built on Forest
Preserve land under Article XIV Section 2 of the Constitution, which
allows not more than three percent of Forest Preserve land to be used
for surface reservoirs for municipal water supply and canals.
However, the water failed drinking water standards and the State
Department of Health ordered the town to either filter the water or
find an alternative ground water supply. By 2005, the water supply
became a serious health and safety problem, elevating levels of
potential carcinogens and causing the Department of Health to warn
residents to boil their drinking water. The only feasible location for
a new water supply was wells on Forest Preserve land; the town could
not afford a filtration plant. Due to the severity of the water
problem, the wells were constructed on Forest Preserve land prior to
the adoption of an authorizing constitutional amendment.

In 2009, the voters approved an amendment authorizing a land exchange
between the State and National Grid, for the construction of a new 46
kV power line across six acres of Forest Preserve land adjoining State
Route 56 in St. Lawrence County. Due to chronic power outages in Lake
Placid, Saranac Lake and Tupper Lake, National Grid was under a
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) order to provide a
redundant power line to service the communities. First legislative
passage of a joint resolution occurred, but after the legislature
adjourned it was discovered that the resolution contained a fatal flaw
and first passage would need to be secured in the next legislative
session. This delay in the amendment process meant that the amendment
could not be passed in time to meet a deadline set forth in the FERC
order. The power line was then constructed without constitutional
authorization, which was subsequently acquired.

It is unreasonable that these basic projects cannot move forward
without individual amendments to the state constitution. Similar
amendments authorizing the use of State land are not required anywhere
else in the state.

The proposal should not, however, result in the widespread misuse of
state lands. All projects will need to be approved by DEC after public
review and comment, and any project can be denied by DEC if a feasible
alternative to the use of state land exist, environmental impacts
aren't minimized by the use of state land, or the state land has
critical environmental or recreational value.

The acreage contained in the land bank is also limited: 250 acres in
the Catskill region and 500 acres in the Adirondack region. No
individual project may use more than five acres of land. Without
specific authorizing legislation, no town could utilize in total more
than ten acres, and no county could utilize more than 15 acres.
Moreover, the proposal requires that the integrity of the forest
preserve be protected: project proponents would be required to pay the
State the appraised value of the state land to be utilized, which
payment would be deposited in the existing forest preserve expansion
fund. And the State will acquire land that will be classified as
wilderness - the most restrictive land classification - in advance of
allowing the land bank to be used, in addition to forest preserve
acquisition using the funds received for utilization of the land bank.

The amendment and this accompanying implementing legislation would
only serve to eliminate constitutional restrictions on the siting of
certain types of projects on State lands in Forest Preserve counties;
other applicable law is not being overridden. The State Environmental
Quality Review Act, the wetlands act, the rivers act, the Adirondack
Park Agency Act, the Clean Water Act, and all other laws which are not
inconsistent with the provisions of this constitutional amendment will
continue to apply to all projects.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is a new bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
This would result in increased funding to be available for the
acquisition of new lands for the Forest Preserve.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the same date and in the same manner as
a "CONCURRENT RESOLUTION OF THE SENATE AND ASSEMBLY proposing an
amendment to article 14 of the constitution, in relation to
establishing a forest preserve land bank for public projects" takes
effect, in accordance with section 1 of article 19 of the
constitution.

summary: Enacts legislation implementing the provisions of a constitutional amendment authorizing public utility lines and bike paths to be located within the forest preserve, and establishes land banks within such preserve for public projects.
title: Enacts legislation to implement a constitutional amendment authorizing the placement of public utility line and bike paths in the forest preserve and establishing land banks
